newsitem.title: USA: Polygram's Motown head to leave in reshuffle - sources.
newsitem.headline: Polygram's Motown head to leave in reshuffle - sources.

text.p: Soul music label Motown Records, which has seen its market share slide due to a lack of hits in recent years, is about to announce a reorganization that includes the dismissal of Chief Executive Officer Andre Harrell, music industry sources said Friday.
Officials at PolyGram NV, which acquired Motown in 1993, declined to comment.

The details of the reorganization are still being negotiated, the sources said. But the shake-up is expected to involve the promotion of industry veteran Danny Goldberg, president of PolyGram's Mercury Records unit, to a broader role overseeing several of its U.S. music labels, including Motown.
"They need someone to come in to clean house," said one record industry executive who requested anonymity.
Another industry executive who declined to be identified said Harrell's departure was imminent and that final details of his exit package were being worked out.

Industry sources said that Harrell, who has been criticized for his lavish spending habits while racking up sizable losses at the legendary label, will receive a hefty severance package. Harrell is in the second of five years in a multi-million contract.
In its heyday in the 1960s, Motown made household names of the first wave of pop-soul stars Stevie Wonder, Smokey Robinson, Diana Ross and The Supremes, The Four Tops and The Temptations.

But its U.S. market share has shrunk to under 1 percent in recent years, as its aging store of artists met with stiff competition from both established labels and upstart operations that cater to young, urban audiences.

Goldberg has been credited with turning Mercury into one of PolyGram's crown jewels by signing such hit acts as the teenage trio Hanson, which has sold more than three million records. A spokeswoman for Goldberg declined to comment.
Sources said they also expect staff and artist cutbacks to accompany the Motown reorganization.

"Reducing overhead is what is helping to shore up industry profitability, and therefore we expect to see more overhead reduction and layoffs in the future," said John Penney, an analyst with Sanford C. Bernstein & Co. Inc.

Penney added: "In a more competitive enviroment when a label share is weak, the industry's first response is to change the top management. This can re-energize a label, though there's no assurance that it will."
